cards.objective: Name the vessel bringing absorbed nutrients to the liver.
cards.front: Which vessel brings nutrient-rich blood from the gut to the liver?

why.t: The hepatic portal vein brings nutrient-rich blood from the gut. It supplies more oxygen than the hepatic artery. Hepatocytes, about 80 percent of its volume, line porous sinusoids and process what the blood brings.

simpler.t: Your liver is a big organ under your right ribs. It makes bile and cleans your blood.

depth.t: Right and left lobes: a large right lobe and a much smaller left lobe.
Quadrate and caudate lobes: smaller lobes some anatomists identify within the right lobe.
Falciform ligament: a remnant of the umbilical vein that separates the right and left lobes in front.
Porta hepatis: the “gate” where the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein enter.

clinical.t: A blockage that stops bile reaching the intestine. Without bile, fats are not emulsified and bilirubin does not colour the stool.

trap.t: The portal vein, not the smaller hepatic artery, supplies most of the liver’s oxygen.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 23.6 Accessory Organs in Digestion: The Liver, Pancreas, and Gallbladder

cards.objective: Name the islet cells that make glucagon.
cards.front: Which pancreatic islet cells make glucagon?

why.t: In each islet, beta cells (insulin) make up about 75 percent and alpha cells (glucagon) about 20 percent. Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.

simpler.t: Your pancreas makes juices to digest food and insulin to manage sugar in your blood.

depth.t: Head, body and tail: head in the duodenal curve, body extending left, tail at the hilum of the spleen.
Acini: grape-like clusters of cells that make pancreatic juice.
Pancreatic islets: islands of endocrine cells among the acini (formerly the islets of Langerhans).
Pancreatic ducts: the main duct joins the bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

clinical.t: Protein-digesting enzymes activated inside the pancreas. Active enzymes digest the pancreatic tissue.
clinical.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The symptoms of pancreatitis.

trap.t: Beta cells make insulin, which lowers blood glucose; alpha cells make glucagon, which raises it.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 23.6 Accessory Organs in Digestion; 17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

cards.objective: List the features that enlarge the absorptive surface of the small intestine.
cards.front: Which three features enlarge the absorptive surface of the small intestine?

why.t: Circular folds, villi and microvilli increase its absorptive surface more than 600-fold. Each villus holds a capillary bed and a lacteal, so absorbed nutrients pass straight into blood or lymph.

simpler.t: Your small intestine is a long, coiled tube that takes the goodness from your food.

depth.t: Duodenum: the shortest part, about 25 cm.
Ileum: the longest part, about 1.8 m.
Circular folds: deep ridges of mucosa and submucosa that make chyme spiral and slow down.
Villi and microvilli: finger-like projections and their tiny surface extensions, the brush border.

clinical.t: Too little lactase made by the absorptive cells. Bacteria in the large intestine ferment the undigested lactose, making gas.

trap.t: Villi are projections of the mucosa; microvilli are extensions of single cells (the brush border).

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 23.5 The Small and Large Intestines

cards.objective: Name the gastric cells that secrete acid.
cards.front: Which cells of the gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid?

why.t: Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells make pepsinogen. Mucus rich in bicarbonate, tight junctions and fast cell renewal protect the stomach from digesting itself.

simpler.t: Your stomach stores a meal and mixes it with acid juices before passing it on.

depth.t: Cardia: where the oesophagus joins and food enters.
Fundus: the dome above and to the left of the cardia, under the diaphragm.
Body: the main part of the stomach.
Pylorus: the funnel to the duodenum, ending at the pyloric sphincter, which controls emptying.
Rugae: large folds of mucosa and submucosa that form when the stomach is empty.

clinical.t: Long use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin, or Helicobacter pylori infection. Gastric juice eats deeper into the unprotected mucosa.

trap.t: Chief cells make pepsinogen; the parietal cells’ acid converts it into pepsin.
